proposals.name: Curiosity gap
proposals.rationale: Uncertainty can motivate clicks independently of conventional news value.
proposals.description: High when the headline withholds a salient answer while supplying enough context to invite discovery; low when fully resolved. Does not apply when no meaningful information is withheld.

proposals.name: Explanatory promise
proposals.rationale: Readers may click for understanding, not just event importance.
proposals.description: High when the headline promises to explain causes, mechanisms, implications, or background; low when it merely reports an event. Does not apply without explanatory framing.

proposals.name: Personal stakes
proposals.rationale: Direct self-interest is a distinct readership motive from aggregate economic or political impact.
proposals.description: High when ordinary readers’ safety, health, rights, income, or daily choices are directly implicated; low when consequences are remote. Does not apply without a plausible individual consequence.

proposals.name: Emotional arousal
proposals.rationale: Strong affect can attract readership even when formal news values are weak.
proposals.description: High when wording clearly evokes fear, anger, grief, joy, awe, or relief; low when emotionally neutral. Does not apply when no emotional response is reasonably cued.

proposals.name: Norm violation
proposals.rationale: Perceived wrongdoing creates attention beyond violence, crisis, or legal-process labels.
proposals.description: High when the headline signals a breach of moral, legal, or social expectations; low when behavior is routine or legitimate. Does not apply without an identifiable norm.

proposals.name: Polarized contestation
proposals.rationale: Polarization can increase readership through identity threat and disagreement.
proposals.description: High when opposing groups, accusations, rebuttals, or incompatible positions are explicit; low when there is no dispute. Does not apply to uncontested claims.

proposals.name: Accountability attribution
proposals.rationale: Readers attend to answerability, a dimension separate from merely reporting institutional action.
proposals.description: High when responsibility, blame, or culpability is assigned to an identifiable party; low when events lack attribution. Does not apply when the headline makes no causal or moral assignment.

proposals.name: Narrative suspense
proposals.rationale: Anticipation can sustain clicks even absent exceptional scale or recency.
proposals.description: High when an unfolding situation leaves the next development uncertain; low when the headline states a settled endpoint. Does not apply without a discernible sequence or unresolved trajectory.

proposals.name: Resolution payoff
proposals.rationale: Outcome satisfaction can make otherwise ordinary stories compelling.
proposals.description: High when the headline signals rescue, reversal, vindication, revelation, or another satisfying outcome; low when it offers only setup. Does not apply when no outcome is indicated.

proposals.name: Concrete scene vividness
proposals.rationale: Imageable situations may attract attention without relying on violence or celebrity.
proposals.description: High when the headline presents a specific, easily imagined scene, action, or object; low when it remains abstract. Does not apply when no scene or action is described.

proposals.name: Ordinary-person agency
proposals.rationale: Agency adds human salience not captured by elite actors or institutional action.
proposals.description: High when a non-elite individual makes a consequential choice or takes decisive action; low when people are passive subjects. Does not apply without an individual decision or action.

proposals.name: Practical actionability
proposals.rationale: Readers may click for immediate guidance rather than narrative interest.
proposals.description: High when the headline helps readers decide what to do, avoid, or prepare for; low when it offers no usable implication. Does not apply to non-advisory stories.

proposals.name: Interpretive accessibility
proposals.rationale: Comprehensible headlines reduce the effort required to become a reader.
proposals.description: High when meaning is immediately clear in ordinary language; low when jargon, ambiguity, or unexplained references obstruct comprehension. Does not apply when the headline is too incomplete to interpret.

proposals.name: Exclusive-access cue
proposals.rationale: Perceived privileged access can increase clicks independently of topic-level news values.
proposals.description: High when wording signals firsthand testimony, newly obtained material, or unusual access; low when it presents a generic summary. Does not apply without an access or exclusivity claim.

proposals.name: Conversation potential
proposals.rationale: Social currency can amplify readership beyond the article’s formal newsworthiness.
proposals.description: High when the headline is likely to prompt discussion or sharing because it is provocative, surprising, identity-relevant, or relatable; low when socially inert. Does not apply to strictly private or technical content.

proposals.name: Headline word count
proposals.description: Count the whitespace-delimited words, excluding the headline label. This captures slot, template, and desk-length conventions rather than reader appeal.

proposals.name: Question or explainer framing
proposals.description: Mark headlines beginning with “why,” “how,” “what,” or “did,” or explicitly using “explaining.” This may signal an explainer package or search-oriented format.

proposals.name: First-person or quoted voice
proposals.description: Mark a headline containing a first-person quotation or a quoted personal statement. This can identify feature commissioning and human-interest packaging.

proposals.name: Leading geographic dateline
proposals.description: Mark headlines that begin with “In” followed by a place, or with a country or city name. This can reveal foreign-desk or bureau-origin conventions.

proposals.name: Institutional action boilerplate
proposals.description: Mark headlines using an institution or office as the grammatical actor with verbs such as “condemns,” “announces,” “sentences,” “denies,” or “accuses.” This identifies official-feed and beat templates.

proposals.name: Entertainment role labels
proposals.description: Mark explicit entertainment labels such as “star,” “comedian,” “pop star,” “Friends fame,” or “rock royalty.” These identify entertainment-oriented desk packaging.

proposals.name: Exact quantities or figures
proposals.parent: data, science, health, or impact-reporting desk
proposals.description: Mark headlines containing numerals, percentages, durations, counts, or precise quantities such as “42 years” or “25%.” This may reflect data-heavy desk templates.

proposals.name: Present-tense headline verbs
proposals.description: Mark headlines whose main event verb is present tense, such as “kills,” “aims,” “misses,” or “announces.” This can reflect house style and publication timing.

proposals.name: Calendar or seasonal cues
proposals.description: Mark explicit months, years, seasons, named scheduled events, or timing phrases such as “in August 2019,” “summer,” or “amid Covid-19.” These can encode the surrounding news cycle.

proposals.name: Running-story continuation markers
proposals.description: Mark words such as “latest,” “again,” “still,” “keeps,” “return,” or “deadline” that imply continuation from earlier coverage. These can reveal persistence or position within a multi-day package.

proposals.name: Open information loop
proposals.rationale: Readers click to resolve questions or discover omitted information.
proposals.description: High when the headline poses a why/how/what question or withholds a salient answer; low when it gives a fully resolved account; it does not apply when no information gap is inferable

proposals.name: Narrative reversal
proposals.rationale: Compact story arcs motivate readers to follow the outcome.
proposals.description: High when it contrasts an earlier condition with a changed outcome or status; low when it reports an ordinary event without a before-and-after turn; it does not apply without temporal comparison

proposals.name: Explicit emotional language
proposals.rationale: Explicit affect attracts attention even when conventional news values are weak.
proposals.description: High when it names strong feelings or reactions; low when wording is neutral; it does not apply when emotion is only implied by the subject matter

proposals.name: Normative judgment
proposals.rationale: Moral language signals stakes and invites readers to assess what happened.
proposals.description: High when the headline makes a moral or evaluative judgment; low when it reports descriptively; it does not apply without evaluative language

proposals.name: Identity polarization
proposals.rationale: Group conflict activates identity-based attention beyond institutional importance.
proposals.description: High when it contrasts social, ethnic, national, partisan, or ideological groups; low when no group opposition appears; it does not apply without identity framing

proposals.name: Personal testimony
proposals.rationale: First-person experience increases intimacy and perceived relevance.
proposals.description: High when it uses first-person language or an individual’s direct experience; low when it is impersonal; it does not apply without a personal voice

proposals.name: Practical service promise
proposals.rationale: Direct utility provides an independent reason to read.
proposals.description: High when the headline promises advice, instructions, or help with a decision; low when it offers no usable guidance; it does not apply without a service frame

proposals.name: Personal welfare stakes
proposals.rationale: Perceived personal consequences can drive readership beyond national importance.
proposals.description: High when it signals direct effects on people’s health, safety, rights, or daily routines; low when consequences remain remote or institutional; it does not apply without individual consequences

proposals.name: Visual or multimedia cue
proposals.rationale: Visual affordances create an immediate click motive.
proposals.description: High when it offers images/video or describes a vivid observable scene or object; low when it is abstract; it does not apply without a media or scene cue

proposals.name: Quantitative precision
proposals.rationale: Precise figures make claims concrete and memorable.
proposals.description: High when it includes an exact number, proportion, duration, or measurable threshold; low when amounts are vague; it does not apply without quantification

proposals.name: Explanatory framing
proposals.rationale: Explanation attracts readers seeking understanding rather than updates.
proposals.description: High when it promises causes, mechanisms, or background; low when it merely announces an event or outcome; it does not apply without an explanatory promise

proposals.name: Semantic completeness
proposals.rationale: Clear packaging reduces comprehension friction and supports informed clicking.
proposals.description: High when the main actor, action, and object or result are plainly stated; low when it relies on vague pronouns, omissions, or unclear syntax; it does not apply without a propositional claim

proposals.name: Figurative wording
proposals.rationale: Nonliteral phrasing increases memorability and attention.
proposals.description: High when it uses a metaphor, idiom, pun, or other clear nonliteral phrase; low when wording is literal; it does not apply without figurative language

proposals.name: Cross-domain juxtaposition
proposals.rationale: Unexpected combinations broaden appeal and create curiosity.
proposals.description: High when it connects two normally distinct domains; low when it stays within one domain; it does not apply when no domain contrast is clear

proposals.name: Hopeful or prosocial resolution
proposals.rationale: Positive closure attracts readers through hope, relief, or prosocial interest.
proposals.description: High when it ends with rescue, recovery, aid, reconciliation, exoneration, or another positive outcome; low when the ending is negative or neutral; it does not apply without an outcome or valence

proposals.name: HEADLINE COMPRESSION
proposals.description: 7 words or fewer | DESCRIPTION: Count whitespace-separated words and flag headlines with seven or fewer. PARENT: mobile-card space constraints

proposals.name: QUESTION-FORM PACKAGING
proposals.description: Begins with a question word and ends with a question mark | DESCRIPTION: Flag headlines beginning with “why,” “how,” “what,” or “did” and ending in “?”. PARENT: explainer/SEO packaging workflow

proposals.name: QUOTE-LED FORM
proposals.description: Contains a direct quotation | DESCRIPTION: Flag headlines containing quotation marks around an attributed or reported phrase. PARENT: statement-led breaking-news workflow

proposals.name: COLON-SPLIT STRUCTURE
proposals.description: Contains a headline colon | DESCRIPTION: Flag headlines using a colon to divide a teaser from an explanatory clause. PARENT: BBC house-style template

proposals.name: VAGUE REFERENT
proposals.description: Uses an underspecified central noun | DESCRIPTION: Flag terms such as “something,” “problem,” or “biggest news” when the headline withholds the specific referent. PARENT: click-oriented homepage packaging

proposals.name: NUMERIC TOKEN
proposals.description: Contains an explicit quantity | DESCRIPTION: Flag any digit or spelled-out number referring to an age, count, percentage, duration, or deadline. PARENT: data, legal, or crisis desk

proposals.name: LOCATION-FIRST LEAD
proposals.description: Starts with a place name | DESCRIPTION: Flag headlines beginning with a geographic name or with “In” followed by a place. PARENT: international/local desk allocation

proposals.name: NAMED-ENTITY DENSITY
proposals.description: Contains two or more named entities | DESCRIPTION: Count distinct named people, organizations, countries, cities, or brands appearing in the headline. PARENT: elite-actor or celebrity beat assignment

proposals.name: FRESHNESS DEICTICS
proposals.description: Uses explicit freshness words | DESCRIPTION: Flag words such as “new,” “latest,” “today,” “now,” “just,” or “still.” PARENT: time-of-day and news-cycle timing

proposals.name: CONTINUATION CUE
proposals.description: Signals a prior installment | DESCRIPTION: Flag explicit sequence language such as “latest,” “again,” “returns,” “in a row,” or “after,” when it refers to an ongoing story. PARENT: multi-day running-story order

proposals.name: PERSONAL STAKES
proposals.rationale: Readers click when consequences feel personally relevant, even if the event lacks elite, crisis, scale, or economic-news prominence.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline states a direct effect on ordinary people’s safety, health, money, rights, or daily life; low when consequences are remote or abstract. It does not apply when no affected people or concrete stake is identifiable

proposals.name: ACTIONABILITY
proposals.rationale: Practical usefulness can motivate readership independently of institutional action, recency, or dramatic event characteristics.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline gives readers a concrete decision, precaution, benefit, or next step; low when it only describes events. It does not apply when no reader-facing implication is stated

proposals.name: CURIOSITY GAP
proposals.rationale: Unanswered questions create an information-seeking motive that standard news-value categories may miss.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline withholds a central explanation, cause, or consequence; low when it provides a complete, straightforward summary. It does not apply when no meaningful unanswered element is present

proposals.name: UNRESOLVED OUTCOME
proposals.rationale: Uncertain outcomes sustain attention because readers want resolution, even without crisis, violence, or legal proceedings.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline signals that an outcome remains contingent or unfolding; low when the result is settled. It does not apply to static background or stories lacking temporal progression

proposals.name: RELATIONAL CONFLICT
proposals.rationale: Relational disputes attract attention through interpersonal stakes without qualifying as violence, institutional action, or legal news.
proposals.description: Scores high when people or groups are explicitly shown disagreeing, blaming, competing, or experiencing interpersonal tension; low when relationships are cooperative or neutral. It does not apply when conflict is only implied by a violent event

proposals.name: POLARIZATION
proposals.rationale: Polarization increases attention by making a story socially discussable beyond listed actor and crisis categories.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline presents opposing camps or a divisive proposition; low when it describes consensus or a technical matter. It does not apply when disagreement is not explicitly stated

proposals.name: TRUST VIOLATION
proposals.rationale: Perceived betrayal invites judgment and discussion without requiring formal corruption, criminality, or court action.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline explicitly signals betrayal, deception, hypocrisy, or concealment; low when it describes routine error or disagreement. It does not apply when wrongdoing is only inferred

proposals.name: AFFECTIVE INTENSITY
proposals.rationale: Explicit emotional charge can drive clicks even when the event is not violent, catastrophic, or celebrity-centered.
proposals.description: Scores high when strongly emotional words or quoted emotion are central; low when wording is emotionally neutral. It does not apply when intensity comes solely from the event category without emotive language

proposals.name: EXPLANATORY PROMISE
proposals.rationale: Explanatory headlines serve readers’ desire for understanding, distinct from simply reporting consequential events.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline promises explanation through “why,” “how,” “what do we know,” or equivalent wording; low when it only reports an event. It does not apply when explanatory intent is absent

proposals.name: INFORMATION SPECIFICITY
proposals.rationale: Concrete details improve perceived relevance and curiosity, while vague wording can suppress clicks despite strong nominal news values.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline supplies concrete people, places, numbers, objects, and actions; low when wording is vague or generic. It does not apply when the subject itself cannot reasonably be made more specific

proposals.name: PROCESSING FLUENCY
proposals.rationale: Easy parsing lowers recognition effort; difficult syntax or jargon may deter otherwise interested readers.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline is immediately understandable with familiar wording and syntax; low when jargon, ambiguity, or complexity slows comprehension. It does not apply when specialized terminology is unavoidable

proposals.name: CREDIBILITY CUES
proposals.rationale: Attribution and evidence markers can increase trust and click motivation independently of topic prominence.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline includes attribution, data, records, eyewitnesses, or other evidence markers; low when it presents unsupported claims. It does not apply when the claim is inherently self-evident

proposals.name: VISUALIZABLE SCENE
proposals.rationale: Vivid scenes can attract attention without depending on violence, novelty, celebrity, or scale.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline depicts a concrete, easily imagined scene or action; low when it describes an abstract condition or process. It does not apply when no scene or action is presented

proposals.name: SOCIAL IDENTIFICATION
proposals.rationale: Identification can motivate group members even when a story lacks domestic relevance or individualized human-interest framing.
proposals.description: Scores high when an explicitly named group can readily see itself represented or affected; low when no identifiable social constituency is invoked. It does not apply when group relevance is merely inferred

proposals.name: PRIOR-KNOWLEDGE DEPENDENCE
proposals.rationale: Context dependence can invite follow-up from invested readers or reduce accessibility, making it a meaningful headline-level signal.
proposals.description: Scores high when understanding the headline requires background supplied by an earlier story; low when its meaning is self-contained. It does not apply when all necessary context appears in the headline

proposals.name: Headline brevity
proposals.parent: headline template or homepage slot constraints
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Count the headline's whitespace-separated words; classify as present when there are eight or fewer.

proposals.name: Question-led framing
proposals.description: begins with Why, How, Did, or What | DESCRIPTION: Mark headlines beginning with an interrogative word or ending in a question mark.

proposals.name: Quote-led formatting
proposals.description: opening quotation mark | DESCRIPTION: Mark headlines whose first character is a quotation mark or whose main wording is a quoted utterance.

proposals.name: Personal-voice framing
proposals.description: first-person wording | DESCRIPTION: Mark headlines containing “I,” “we,” or an explicitly personal testimony framed in the speaker's own voice.

proposals.name: Image-package wording
proposals.parent: multimedia package or homepage visual slot
proposals.description: visual-media reference | DESCRIPTION: Mark headlines explicitly mentioning a photo, image, images, video, or visual gallery.

proposals.name: Institutional abbreviation
proposals.description: acronym or initialism | DESCRIPTION: Mark headlines containing an all-capital abbreviation of at least two letters, such as UN, NHS, or PM.

proposals.name: Location-heavy wording
proposals.description: named geography | DESCRIPTION: Mark headlines containing two or more explicit countries, cities, regions, or national demonyms.

proposals.name: Procedural legal verbs
proposals.description: formal case language | DESCRIPTION: Mark headlines using terms such as arrested, charged, sentenced, appeal, exonerated, or surrender deadline.

proposals.name: Continuation cues
proposals.description: running-story language | DESCRIPTION: Mark headlines containing cues such as latest, again, return, amid, as, keeps, or ramp up that imply an ongoing story.

proposals.name: Numerical framing
proposals.description: prominent figures or counts | DESCRIPTION: Mark headlines containing a percentage, explicit count, age, duration, date, or ordinal number.

proposals.name: Curiosity Gap
proposals.rationale: Unresolved questions and withheld answers can motivate clicks independently of elite status, crisis, novelty, or recency.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline withholds a salient answer while clearly promising one; low when it states the complete takeaway. It does not apply when no meaningful information is withheld.

proposals.name: Self-Contained Comprehensibility
proposals.rationale: Readers are less likely to click when they cannot identify the story’s subject or significance from the headline alone.
proposals.description: Scores high when the actor, event, setting, and significance are clear without prior context; low when vague references or missing essentials block understanding. It does not apply when the headline makes no substantive claim.

proposals.name: Narrative Tension
proposals.rationale: Unresolved opposition creates a reason to follow the developing outcome.
proposals.description: Scores high when identifiable parties pursue incompatible aims or an outcome remains pending; low when there is no opposition or the outcome is settled. It does not apply to a single actor or static event.

proposals.name: Surprise or Reversal
proposals.rationale: Reversals and paradoxes attract attention without requiring crisis, celebrity, or elite actors.
proposals.description: Scores high when an apparent expectation is overturned or two elements form a striking paradox; low when the development is routine or expected. It does not apply when no unexpected relationship is conveyed.

proposals.name: Emotional Intensity
proposals.rationale: Strongly signaled emotions can increase attention independently of the underlying news category.
proposals.description: Scores high when wording clearly signals strong fear, anger, joy, grief, awe, or disgust; low when emotionally neutral. It does not apply when no clear emotional valence is inferable.

proposals.name: Moral Norm Violation
proposals.rationale: Norm violations invite moral judgment and attention even without violence, legal proceedings, or crisis.
proposals.description: Scores high when conduct or an outcome clearly violates a widely shared moral norm; low when conduct is ordinary or benign. It does not apply when evaluation depends on facts absent from the headline.

proposals.name: Ideological Polarization
proposals.rationale: Ideological stakes can mobilize readership through disagreement and identity.
proposals.description: Scores high when opposing political, religious, national, or moral camps are identifiable; low when disagreement is technical or no stance is present. It does not apply when group positions are not explicit.

proposals.name: Practical Utility
proposals.rationale: Utility gives readers a direct reason to click for understanding or action.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline offers advice, explanation, or decision guidance readers can use; low when it merely reports an event. It does not apply when no practical takeaway is stated.

proposals.name: Concrete Scene Vividness
proposals.rationale: Vivid scenes are easier to imagine and remember, supporting clicks without scale or elite status.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline depicts a specific sensory scene, object, or action that is readily pictured; low when wording is abstract or bureaucratic. It does not apply when no concrete scene is conveyed.

proposals.name: Distinctive Voice
proposals.rationale: A distinctive human voice can make a headline memorable beyond topic-based news values.
proposals.description: Scores high when first-person language, a memorable phrase, or an unusual quotation sounds like a person speaking; low when phrasing is generic and institutional. It does not apply when the wording is not clearly voice-driven.

proposals.name: Source Transparency
proposals.rationale: Visible sourcing can build trust and clarify why a claim merits attention.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline identifies a source, evidence, or attribution that clarifies claim provenance; low when it presents an unsupported assertion. It does not apply to plainly observable events without contested claims.

proposals.name: Epistemic Uncertainty
proposals.rationale: Uncertainty can prompt readers to seek clarification without a dramatic event.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline explicitly signals denial, dispute, uncertainty, or incomplete knowledge; low when it presents a settled account. It does not apply when neither a factual claim nor uncertainty cue is present.

proposals.name: Visual-Content Promise
proposals.rationale: A promised visual experience can independently motivate clicks when the text itself is sparse.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline explicitly promises images, video, live updates, maps, or interactive material; low when no media experience is suggested. It does not apply when no format cue appears.

proposals.name: Social-Identity Resonance
proposals.rationale: Identity cues can make stories personally consequential to many readers without requiring domestic relevance.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline invokes a shared group identity, belonging, or identity-related value; low when no group identity is implicated. It does not apply when relevance requires personal details absent from the headline.

proposals.name: Humorous or Playful Framing
proposals.rationale: Playfulness can increase entertainment value and curiosity apart from celebrity or human-interest framing.
proposals.description: Scores high when wording uses an unambiguous joke, pun, irony, or comic incongruity; low when it is sober and literal. It does not apply when humor is not clearly signaled.

proposals.name: Headline brevity
proposals.description: Count the headline’s words or characters; unusually short headlines may reflect compact homepage slots or stronger promotion.

proposals.name: Question framing
proposals.description: Mark headlines ending in a question mark or beginning with “Why,” “How,” or “Did.” This may identify explainer formats favored by particular desks or slots.

proposals.name: Quoted speech
proposals.description: Mark headlines containing quotation marks around a phrase or sentence. Quoted headlines may fingerprint interview, reaction, or live-news formats.

proposals.name: First-person testimony
proposals.description: Mark explicit first-person wording such as “I,” “we,” or “my.” This may identify human-interest packages or feature treatment.

proposals.name: Celebrity-name presence
proposals.description: Mark prominent entertainers, influencers, athletes, or royals named in the headline. Such names may proxy an audience-specific desk or cross-site promotion.

proposals.name: Numerical specificity
proposals.description: Mark digits, percentages, ages, counts, or precise quantities. This may fingerprint data-led, health, or breaking-news treatments.

proposals.name: Institutional action verbs
proposals.description: Mark verbs such as “announces,” “condemns,” “sentences,” “sanctions,” or “removes.” These may identify institutionally prioritized coverage and its standard headline templates.

proposals.name: Geographic proper-noun density
proposals.description: Count countries, cities, regions, and nationality adjectives in the headline. Dense geographic marking may proxy international desks, correspondent availability, or homepage allocation.

proposals.name: Recency markers
proposals.parent: Time of capture and seasonal news cycle
proposals.description: Mark words such as “latest,” “new,” “today,” “now,” or “as … burn.” These can reveal the time-sensitive news cycle or when the item entered the homepage run.

proposals.name: Running-story recap framing
proposals.description: Mark “what do we know,” “explaining,” “why …,” “latest images,” or similar recap language. Such wording may fingerprint a later position in a multi-day story or a designated explainer slot.

proposals.name: Curiosity-gap teaser
proposals.rationale: Readers click to resolve the gap; editorial values don't credit withholding.
proposals.description: Headline withholds key entity or fact via demonstratives ("this photo", "biggest news wasn't about X") or quoted mystery. Scores high when withheld element is the hook; low when headline states facts plainly; N/A if no withholding present

proposals.name: Named-individual human drama
proposals.rationale: Personal stories drive reader clicks beyond standard human-interest scoring.
proposals.description: Headline centres one named or individually-described ordinary person's ordeal (fishermen, evacuees, Richard). High for personal narratives; low for statistics or institutions; N/A when no individual present

proposals.name: Second-person or relatable proximity
proposals.rationale: Readers click what touches them personally, regardless of news value.
proposals.description: Headline implies everyday relevance to reader's own life (NHS funding, coronavirus, oxygen). High when outcome affects readers directly; low for distant elites; N/A when topic is foreign-only

proposals.name: Mystery-death novelty
proposals.rationale: Unresolved oddities strongly provoke clicks; articulated scale underweights novelty.
proposals.description: Unexplained death with eerie phrasing ("something in room"). High for unexplained cause plus strangeness; low for routine deaths; N/A when cause is stated

proposals.name: Royal-family personal revelation
proposals.rationale: Royals combine celebrity with domestic relevance; a known click driver.
proposals.description: Headline about royals' private feelings or family conflict. High for first-person feeling words; low for ceremonial duties; N/A for non-royals

proposals.name: YouTube-influencer crossover
proposals.rationale: Digital-native fame drives clicks invisible to traditional celebrity criteria.
proposals.description: Headline names internet celebrities known primarily to younger audiences (KSI, Logan Paul). High when both fame source is online and event is a clash; low for legacy-only celebs; N/A otherwise

proposals.name: Graphic-violence-outrage loop
proposals.rationale: Viral outrage content draws clicks; violence criteria alone miss it.
proposals.description: Headline references shocking attack plus public outrage reaction. High when both attack and outrage appear; low when only one; N/A otherwise

proposals.name: Reader-identity group cue
proposals.rationale: Identity-invoking stories spur clicks from affected or defensive readers.
proposals.description: Headline names a group readers may belong to or feel judged by (parents, anti-Semitism, race disparity). High for group plus evaluative claim; low for neutral policy; N/A when no group named

proposals.name: Explainer-service framing
proposals.rationale: Utility and uncertainty drive information-seeking clicks during running stories.
proposals.description: Headline asks a question or promises explanation ("What do we know?", "How will we know..."). High for question marks or "how/why/what"; low for declarative news; N/A otherwise

proposals.name: Distant-country empathy barrier
proposals.rationale: Articulated criteria over-credit institutional action; readers click domestic-adjacent news.
proposals.description: Story located in a country culturally distant from UK audience with no UK link. High barrier when all actors/places are such; low when UK angle exists; N/A when location unclear

proposals.name: Long-running-story familiarity
proposals.rationale: Cumulative audience familiarity predicts clicks; recency criterion alone misses it.
proposals.description: Headline references a story with prior wide coverage (Trump, Covid, Lula). High when proper noun already heavily covered; low for first-mention figures; N/A for generic events

proposals.name: Animal-or-child innocence hook
proposals.rationale: Warm novelty stories overperform clicks relative to editorial weight.
proposals.description: Headline features a child, animal, or lost-toy innocence element with happy resolution. High when both present; low when absent; N/A otherwise

proposals.name: Political-process fatigue cue
proposals.rationale: Articulated instrument over-credits elite process; readers click outcomes, not procedure.
proposals.description: Headline about negotiations, coalitions, meetings, procedure without outcome. High when process-only; low when outcome or conflict is concrete; N/A otherwise

proposals.name: Contrarian-debunk angle
proposals.rationale: Epistemic novelty ("were they wrong?") is clickworthy and under-credited.
proposals.description: Headline promises to overturn or fact-check a prior claim (fact-checked, didn't start then). High for explicit checking words; low for straight reports; N/A otherwise

proposals.name: Medical-body relevance
proposals.rationale: Health threats and remedies reliably drive lay readership.
proposals.description: Headline about health, drugs, or bodily function affecting readers or family (contraceptive pill, Ebola, Covid). High when body/health is the subject; low when health is incidental; N/A otherwise

proposals.name: Follow-up day marker
proposals.description: Headline presupposes prior knowledge via pronouns, possessives or definite reference to an ongoing story (e.g. "Manafort problem", "misses surrender deadline", "fights back in corruption row") with no fresh named event.

proposals.name: Second-day framing cue
proposals.description: Analysis or retrospective phrasing ("Why X lost", "Explaining X", "The biggest news wasn't...") indicating the piece is commentary after a peak event.

proposals.name: Uppercase initialism use
proposals.description: Headline contains an uppercase acronym or short initialism (US, PM, NHS, IS, UN, DR Congo, KSI) signalling hard-news agency copy.

proposals.name: Domestic-UK angle tell
proposals.parent: national desk promotion to domestic audience
proposals.description: Explicit mention of UK, England, or a UK institution (NHS, PM), flagging the home-audience desk whose readership baseline is higher.

proposals.name: Royal-celebrity first-name reference
proposals.description: Famous person referred to by first name or nickname alone (Harry, Malala, Lula, KSI), indicating a personality beat with a pre-existing fanbase.

proposals.name: Question-headline format
proposals.description: Headline is phrased as a question ("What do we know?", "How will we know...?"), a live-rolling-news explainer template.

proposals.name: Quote-in-headlines boilerplate
proposals.description: Headline opens with or embeds a scare-quoted first-person utterance, typical of features and human-interest desks.

proposals.name: Geographic remoteness marker
proposals.parent: world desk beat and lower home-page promotion
proposals.description: Only foreign place names with no domestic or elite-actor anchor (Sri Lanka, Ghana, DR Congo, South Africa), signalling world desk items less clicked by BBC's UK-heavy audience.

proposals.name: Colonic name prefix
proposals.description: Headline uses the "Name: story" format (e.g. "Matthew Perry:", "New coronavirus variant:"), a promotion template for lead-story slots.

proposals.name: Mortality-mystery lexicon
proposals.description: Words like killed, death, deaths, serial killings, skeletons, mass grave denoting death/mystery vocabulary typical of true-crime and disaster beats.

proposals.name: Curiosity gap wording
proposals.rationale: Readers click to resolve the gap; same-outcome clickbait structure drives readership
proposals.description: Headline withholds key fact via question, teaser, or incomplete reveal ("Why X lost", "The biggest news wasn't about Y"). Scores high when withholding is explicit; low for fully informative headlines; not applicable when question is merely rhetorical

proposals.name: Named individual as subject
proposals.rationale: Readers gravitate to person-centred stories over institutional ones
proposals.description: Headline centers on one named person (Harry, Matthew Perry, Manafort, Lula) rather than institution or event. Scores high when person's name leads; low for policy/abstract subjects

proposals.name: Violence against identifiable individuals
proposals.rationale: Personal victim narratives drive clicks more than aggregate conflict
proposals.description: Attack on named/shown victims, especially women or children ("attack on women in restaurant", "couple killed"). Scores high; low for mass/institutional violence; N/A for threats only

proposals.name: Mystery or unexplained death framing
proposals.rationale: Unresolved mystery is a strong click trigger
proposals.description: Unexplained cause, ominous ambiguity ("killed by something in room"). High for puzzling deaths; low when cause is stated

proposals.name: Domestic-UK personal relevance
proposals.rationale: BBC audience skews UK; directly-relevant news gets clicked
proposals.description: Story set in UK affecting ordinary readers' lives (NHS cash, England Covid cases, UK PM). High for UK service/policy news; low for foreign equivalents

proposals.name: Health scare with personal actionability
proposals.rationale: Readers click health news with personal stakes
proposals.description: Health threat readers can act on (covid variant, oxygen need). High when symptoms/spread/safety implied; low for abstract research

proposals.name: Royalty or royal family content
proposals.rationale: Royals are uniquely high-click BBC content regardless of news value
proposals.description: Any Royal Family member as subject. High always; N/A otherwise

proposals.name: Celebrity juxtaposed with misfortune
proposals.rationale: Fame-plus-drama strongly attracts casual readers
proposals.description: Famous person plus tragedy/scandal (Perry's demons, KSI fight, star harmed). High; low for routine celebrity news

proposals.name: US politics as spectator sport
proposals.rationale: Personality-driven US politics outperforms institutional coverage
proposals.description: Trump, Obama/Bush, sanctions, Putin allies framed as conflict drama. High for named antagonists clashing; low for procedural items

proposals.name: Anniversarial or slow-burn context
proposals.rationale: Lack of fresh event may suppress clicks; articulated scale over-credits running stories
proposals.description: Headline referencing ongoing story without new event ("amid Covid-19", "keeps Germany waiting"). High when no fresh hook; low when new event present

proposals.name: Negative-valence emotion words
proposals.rationale: Negativity bias in click behaviour
proposals.description: Explicit negative affect: outrage, fear, lost, brutal, gross, drought. High when strong negative word present; low for neutral headlines

proposals.name: Soft-feature despite hard topic
proposals.rationale: Hard-news criteria over-credit; distant hard news may under-click
proposals.description: Human-interest framing of hard event ("Miraculous return of fishermen", "Evacuated twice"). High when individual lens on distant event; low for straight reports

proposals.name: First-person voice or quote
proposals.rationale: Testimony invites empathy clicks; but protest quotes may signal foreign remoteness
proposals.description: Direct quote or first person in headline ("I cut a carrot", "'Down with the military'"). High for relatable first-person; N/A for official quotes

proposals.name: Novel-consumer-technology or science breakthrough
proposals.rationale: Novel, personally-relevant science over-clicks versus news-value weighting
proposals.description: Sex/drugs/tech/gadgets or scientific firsts (contraceptive pill, fusion). High for body-related novelty; lower for pure physics

proposals.name: Continental remoteness to UK audience
proposals.rationale: Geographic distance from BBC readership reduces clicking; articulated scale misses this
proposals.description: Event in region with weak UK audience ties (DR Congo, Sri Lanka, Ghana, Brazil domestic affairs). High remoteness predicts low clicks; low for UK/Europe/US stories

proposals.name: Follow-up headline ellipticalness
proposals.description: Headline omits full names/events and relies on assumed prior knowledge ("Why Donald Trump lost", "The biggest news wasn't about Manafort"), signalling day 2+ of a running story.

proposals.name: Domestic UK peg prominence
proposals.description: Headline names UK institutions or places (NHS, England, UK PM, Kyiv documents leak) reflecting the UK desk's production and home-audience framing.

proposals.name: Quote-first human voice
proposals.description: Headline opens with a first-person or witness quotation in scare quotes ("'I cut a carrot...'", "'Down with the military!'"), marking feature/interview pieces filed on slower cycles.

proposals.name: Explainer formula markers
proposals.description: Headline uses "Why", "How will we know", "What do we know", "Explaining" or "in three simple ways" — a format template tied to analysis desk timing.

proposals.name: Wire-style compression
proposals.description: Headline uses dense noun-stack, place abbreviation, or agency-style syntax ("S Lanka", "Italy river surge kills nine", "US slaps sanctions"), fingerprinting foreign-desk wire copy.

proposals.name: Celebrity personal-name slot
proposals.description: Headline leads with a bare celebrity name plus colon (Harry:, Matthew Perry:, KSI, Malala), reflecting entertainment desk conventions and promoted sidebar placement.

proposals.name: Novelty-record framing
proposals.description: Headline centres a quirky record, mishap or oddity ("Storm helps plane beat record", "Teddy bear lost in park returned"), typical of off-lead slots on light days.

proposals.name: Continuation demonstratives
proposals.description: Headline uses "this" or definite reference without introduction ("Why this photo with Malala", "The couple blamed"), presupposing a story already promoted earlier.

proposals.name: Breaking-tense verb placement
proposals.description: Headline front-loads a sudden-event verb with day-of timing ("announces", "misses surrender deadline", "ramps up"), fingerprinting morning capture slots near homepage top.

proposals.name: Emotional-adjective headline close
proposals.description: Headline ends with an evaluative or emotive noun/phrase ("deep demons", "outrage", "in fear"), a features-desk house style for long-reads published on set schedules.

proposals.name: First-person voice
proposals.rationale: Personal testimony invites emotional engagement and reader clicks.
proposals.description: Score high when the headline contains a first-person pronoun or quoted speech ('I', 'we', 'our', 'litres and litres'). Score low when it is entirely third-person institutional reporting.

proposals.name: Curiosity gap
proposals.rationale: Withheld referents drive click-through regardless of topic.
proposals.description: Score high when the headline withholds key information the reader must click to resolve ('this photo', 'wasn't about Manafort', 'something in room'). Score low when the headline states its own conclusion.

proposals.name: Named Western celebrity
proposals.rationale: Celebrity name recognition strongly drives reader clicks.
proposals.description: Score high when a globally famous entertainment or royal figure is named or implied (Harry, Matthew Perry, KSI, Logan Paul). Does not apply to politicians or officials.

proposals.name: Non-UK foreign domestic story
proposals.rationale: BBC readership skews UK/US; foreign-only domestic stories underperform editorial news values.
proposals.description: Score high when the story is primarily about events internal to a non-UK country with no UK, US, or elite-global hook (Ghana coup, Sri Lanka grave, Congo Ebola). Score low otherwise.

proposals.name: Body-and-suffering framing
proposals.rationale: Visceral threat and harm cue high reader attention and clicks.
proposals.description: Score high when the headline foregrounds violence, death, or physical harm to identifiable persons ('brutal attack', 'killed', 'harmed'). Score low when harm is abstract or statistical.

proposals.name: Moral-outrage trigger
proposals.rationale: Outrage content is disproportionately clicked and shared.
proposals.description: Score high when headline language implies injustice or norm violation ('outrage', 'unidentified', 'exonerated after 42 years', 'gross'). Score low for neutral procedural reporting.

proposals.name: Question-form headline
proposals.rationale: Questions create an information gap that pulls clicks.
proposals.description: Score high when the headline is phrased as a direct question ('How will we know...', 'What do we know?'). Score low for declarative headlines.

proposals.name: Novelty-plus-celebrity interaction
proposals.rationale: Novelty about known figures compounds two click drivers.
proposals.description: Score high only when an unusual or surprising event involves a famous or elite individual (KSI fight, storm-assisted record, plane record). Score low if novelty involves anonymous actors.

proposals.name: Mundane-relatable action
proposals.rationale: Relatable small-scale human stories draw soft-news readers.
proposals.description: Score high when the headline centres on an everyday, ordinary activity framed as remarkable (cutting a carrot, losing a teddy bear). Score low when actions are institutional or geopolitical.

proposals.name: Named-powerful-actor aggression
proposals.rationale: Named-actor conflict is a reliable top-ten readership magnet.
proposals.description: Score high when one named state or leader takes a hostile action against another ('slaps sanctions', 'ramps up threats', 'accuses'). Score low when no specific actor is named.

proposals.name: Explanation or analysis marker
proposals.rationale: Explainers ride major running stories; dense model may read topic salience instead.
proposals.description: Score high when the headline signals explainer or analytical framing ('Why...', 'Explaining...', 'The rise and fall'). Score low for breaking-event headlines.

proposals.name: Domestic UK number statistic
proposals.rationale: Quantified domestic impact correlates with UK reader clicks.
proposals.description: Score high when the headline contains a concrete UK statistic or magnitude ('jump nearly 25% in England', NHS cash). Score low for foreign-place statistics.

proposals.name: Scare-quoted hedging
proposals.rationale: Hedged quotation marks signal controversy and unresolved mystery, boosting clicks.
proposals.description: Score high when key claim is in scare quotes or hedged ('deceptive', 'unidentified', 'killed by something'), signalling contested or uncertain claim. Score low when claims are unqualified.

proposals.name: Underdog-or-injustice victim
proposals.rationale: Individual-level injustice narrative engages readers more than statistics.
proposals.description: Score high when headline identifies an individual wronged or defying power (wedding couple blamed, athletes defying threats, fishermen lost). Score low when victims are anonymous collectives.

proposals.name: Mystery-death hook
proposals.rationale: Unresolved death mysteries are consistently among most-read items.
proposals.description: Score high when an unexplained death or unexplained cause is the core hook ('something in room', serial killings, radiation spike). Score low when cause of harm is stated.

proposals.name: Colon-attribution prefix
proposals.description: Headline opens with "Name:" tagging a person (Matthew Perry:, Lavrov:, Harry:), a house-style marker for people-desk write-throughs.

proposals.name: Question-headline explainer format
proposals.parent: live page and explainer format desk
proposals.description: Headline is phrased as a question ("How will we know...", "What do we know?"), BBC's live-blog/Q&A template.

proposals.name: Follow-day "Why X happened" frame
proposals.description: Postmortem or analysis framing ("Why Donald Trump lost", "Explaining...") marks day 2+ of a running story, after peak click interest.

proposals.name: Ongoing-saga update verb
proposals.description: Weak update verbs like "ramps up", "misses deadline", "denies" signal incremental entry in an already-old story rather than the breaking item.

proposals.name: In-quote ordinary voice
proposals.description: Quoted first-person speech from a non-public figure ("I cut a carrot...", "'litres and litres'") marks magazine/features commissions.

proposals.name: Geographic qualifier string
proposals.description: Place names stacked as qualifiers ("in DR Congo", "S Lanka", "in New South Wales") typical of foreign-desk copy rarely promoted domestically.

proposals.name: Idyll-vs-menace juxtaposition
proposals.description: Wholesome object paired with threat ("Teddy bear lost", "wedding", "fishermen lost at sea") — human-interest desk formula.

proposals.name: Curiosity-withheld-noun head
proposals.description: Deferred referent ("The biggest news wasn't...", "Why this photo...") — click-formula indexing page tools that inflate clicks.

proposals.name: Familiar-figure-only shorthand
proposals.description: Surname alone (Merkel, Manafort, Lula, Lavrov) presumes reader already tracking the story, marking late-stage running coverage.

proposals.name: Soft-news subject domain lexicon
proposals.description: Wellness/lifestyle/science novelty keywords ("contraceptive pill", "cannabis bubble", "parenting influencer") from specialist vertical desks.

proposals.name: Personal-pronoun first-person framing
proposals.rationale: Reader-click behaviour favours intimate first-person voices.
proposals.description: Headline contains a first-person quote or "I/we/my" voice. Scores high when a named or implied ordinary person speaks; does not apply to institutional quotes

proposals.name: Mystery-gap curiosity trigger
proposals.rationale: Curiosity gaps drive click-through more than news values.
proposals.description: Headline withholds the key fact ("Why X lost", "Did X start...?"). Scores high when a question or unexplained outcome creates an information gap

proposals.name: Named Anglophone celebrity
proposals.rationale: BBC readership skews toward recognisable Anglophone personalities.
proposals.description: Headline names a person famous primarily in UK/US entertainment, sport, or royalty. Scores high for household names; low for foreign politicians

proposals.name: Quoted-speech headline
proposals.rationale: Quoted voices signal human-interest stories readers click.
proposals.description: Headline opens with or contains direct quotation marks around speech. Scores high when the quote is emotional or startling; not for scare-quoted single words

proposals.name: Morbid-oddity death mystery
proposals.rationale: Strange-death narratives are strong click magnets.
proposals.description: Death or injury described with unexplained cause ("something in room", "demons"). Scores high when cause is bizarre/ambiguous; low for routine deaths

proposals.name: Reader-addressing question
proposals.rationale: Direct address invites the reader to click for the answer.
proposals.description: Headline is phrased as a question to the reader ("What do we know?", "How will we know...?"). Scores high; does not apply to reported questions

proposals.name: Domestic-UK bodily proximity
proposals.rationale: Readers click what feels personally near and risky.
proposals.description: Event involves UK residents' bodies, health, or homes. Scores high; low when foreign people are affected however gravely

proposals.name: Explicit emotion word
proposals.rationale: Affective language predicts click behaviour beyond topic.
proposals.description: Headline contains emotion terms (fear, outrage, love, demons, gross). Scores high when emotion is the story; not for neutral reporting

proposals.name: Soft-news self-improvement hook
proposals.rationale: Lifestyle relevance drives clicks not captured by hard-news criteria.
proposals.description: Headline implies a life-lesson or how-to relevance ("first time aged 41", parenting). Scores high for ordinary-life milestones

proposals.name: Denial-of-source structure
proposals.rationale: Contested blame invites readers to adjudicate by clicking.
proposals.description: Headline built as "X denies Y" or accusation-rebuttal. Scores high when denial implies unresolved scandal; low when actor is unfamiliar

proposals.name: Named-entity density overload
proposals.rationale: Cognitive load suppresses clicks; dense model may detect this.
proposals.description: Headline names three or more persons, institutions, or places. Scores low—clicks drop when too many unfamiliar entities must be parsed

proposals.name: Scare-quoted scepticism marker
proposals.rationale: Hedged claims read as process news, less clickable.
proposals.description: Single quoted word casting doubt ('deceptive', 'unidentified', 'no value'). Scores low-to-moderate; hedge weakens urgency

proposals.name: Ongoing-saga continuation cue
proposals.rationale: Top-ten slots go to running stories readers already follow.
proposals.description: Headline presupposes prior knowledge ("ramps up", "fights back", "keeps waiting"). Scores high only when actor is already famous

proposals.name: Innocent-victim injustice arc
proposals.rationale: Injustice-vindication is a reliably high-click narrative.
proposals.description: Ordinary person wrongfully harmed and then vindicated (exonerated, cleared). Scores high; low when victim is anonymous or foreign

proposals.name: Novelty-record superlative
proposals.rationale: Concrete superlatives signal shareable, clickable curiosities.
proposals.description: Headline contains "first", "record", "biggest", or numerical extremity. Scores high when superlative is concrete; not for vague hype

proposals.name: Named-politician surname in headline
proposals.parent: Political desk gets heavy cross-promotion and reader default interest
proposals.description: Headline contains a bare surname or full name of a currently prominent politician (Trump, Putin, Merkel, Lavrov, Obama). Judge scores yes if at least one such proper name appears.

proposals.name: Explicit question-mark headline
proposals.parent: Explainer/live-blog desk writes follow-up items on day 2+ of running stories
proposals.description: Headline ends in a question mark, e.g. "What do we know?" or "Did...start in...?"

proposals.name: "Why X..." explainer opener
proposals.parent: Analysis desk staffing and slow-news-cycle production
proposals.description: Headline begins with the word "Why" or "How", signalling an analytical or background piece rather than a breaking event.

proposals.name: Colon-separated celebrity name prefix
proposals.parent: Entertainment desk house style plus celebrity promotion slots
proposals.description: Headline uses the "Name: Story" colon format, the entertainment/obituary house style (e.g. "Matthew Perry: ...").

proposals.name: First-person quote or apostrophe opener
proposals.parent: Features/first-person desk, weekend scheduling, magazine-style promotion
proposals.description: Headline opens with a quotation mark or contains a first-person pronoun (I, we, our, my) in quotes.

proposals.name: UK-domestic institutional actor mention
proposals.parent: Domestic desk timing matched to UK evening traffic peak
proposals.description: Headline names a UK institution or office (NHS, UK PM, England, Department) without naming a person.

proposals.name: Death-or-arrest verb with number
proposals.parent: Breaking-wire desk publishes within minutes of events; top-story slot
proposals.description: Headline contains a numeric casualty/count ("nine", "six", "42 years") combined with a harm verb (kills, arrested, sentenced).

proposals.name: Novelty-record superlative framing
proposals.parent: Offbeat/quirky desk fills mid-day slots; strong social-share push
proposals.description: Headline contains "record", "first", "biggest", or a surprising-inversion framing (plane beat record via storm).

proposals.name: Multi-day story increment marker
proposals.parent: Position within a running story's lifecycle, day 2+ of coverage
proposals.description: Headline presupposes prior knowledge: uses latest, ramping up, return to, fights back, keeps...waiting, again, or demonstratives ("The biggest news wasn't...") implying an ongoing saga.

proposals.name: Lowercase trailing quote fragment
proposals.parent: Copy-desk house style for home-page teasers on secondary-placed stories
proposals.description: Headline's final words are a quoted fragment in quotes or with scare quotes around one word ('deceptive', 'unidentified', 'No value').
